editor_spans.body: I've already argued (S355) that the Prime Minister's Motherwell speech puts pressure on Holyrood by presenting Westminster as the champion of Scotland's regions. This time I want to look at the one concrete item in the speech, the 'offer of DWP devolution', because it shows what the strategy can and cannot deliver. Most of what Burnham offered is either money Holyrood already partly controls or small sums. There is £10 million for defence colleges, matched by Edinburgh. The £1 billion for research and innovation is spread across the whole UK. And there is a promise to 'explore' giving Scottish regions some say over research funding. Employment support is different. The Department for Work and Pensions is reserved to Westminster. It is the one lever where London actually holds something Edinburgh cannot simply take, which makes it the real bargaining chip.

The offer is vaguer than it sounds. Scotland already runs its own devolved employment programmes, a result of the post-referendum settlement. What it does not control is the core of the benefits system: Jobcentres, Universal Credit and the conditions and sanctions attached to claims. The speech never says whether those are on the table. It promises a model 'similar to the one in England', and English devolution so far has meant mayors commissioning programmes, not running the benefits system. Until the National Economic Council sets out the details, 'DWP devolution' could mean anything from a new commissioning budget to real control over how claimants are treated. Those are very different things.

There is also a tension at the centre of the speech that nobody seems to have noticed. Burnham builds his case on the 'Easterhouse principle': names not numbers, person-centred support, no 'computer says no'. In the same passage he says he 'won't have a country where we get comfortable with the idea of kids in their 20s just being there on benefits', and he points to the Milburn review of young people out of work. The language of trust and the language of tougher expectations sit side by side. The real question for Holyrood is which one comes with the devolved powers. If Scotland is handed the job of delivering employment support while Westminster keeps the benefit rules and sanctions, Edinburgh would take the political blame for a system it still does not design.

The speech is right about the long-term cause. Ravenscraig closed in 1992, and more than thirty years later the site is still being filled. The towns built around coal and steel are still the places with empty high streets, shrinking working populations and gaps in life expectancy. Burnham's own diagnosis is that these decisions were taken 'hundreds of miles away' by people who never lived with the consequences. But his answer is a negotiation between two capitals over who gets to let go. Neither government has yet offered Motherwell or Inverclyde a permanent revenue base of their own. Without one, 'power to the regions' amounts to schemes and pots of money that regions have to bid for, and that is the kind of centralised control the speech says it is against.
